Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Pregnant women in Peru are dying at scandalous rates, according to the author of an Amnesty International report into maternal mortality in the South American country. The report, "Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru" found that hundreds of poor, rural and indigenous pregnant women are dying because they are being denied the same health services as other women in the country. It also concluded that the government's response to tackling the problem was inadequate. Peruvian government figures state 185 in every 100,000 women die in childbirth, but the United Nations says the number is much higher, 240 per 100,000, which makes it one of the highest rates of maternal mortality in the Americas. In wealthy developed nations, only nine women die for every 100,000 births. The five main causes of pregnancy-related deaths in Peru are hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, infection, complications following abortion and obstructed birth, according to Peru's Ministry of Health figures. Amnesty's Peru researcher Nuria Garcia said, in a written statement: "The rates of maternal mortality in Peru are scandalous. The fact that so many women are dying from preventable causes is a human rights violation. "The Peruvian state is simply ignoring its obligation to provide adequate maternal health care to all women, regardless of who they are and where they live." Garcia added: "Health services for pregnant women in Peru are like a lottery: If you are poor and indigenous, the chances are you will always lose." The report said pregnant women in Peru die because they lack access to emergency obstetric care, to information on maternal health, and to health staff members who can speak Indigenous languages such as Quechua -- a native Andean language spoken by some 5 million people in Peru. According to the report, 27 percent of deaths of women from pregnancy-related causes occurred during pregnancy; 26 percent occurred during the birth itself; and 46 percent during the first six weeks after giving birth. A 2007 Census of Indigenous People showed that 60 percent did not have access to a health facility, said Amnesty International. The Amnesty International report notes that the Peruvian government has instituted policies aimed at reducing the rates of maternal mortality, such as increasing maternal waiting houses -- rooms where pregnant women who live far from health centers can stay. Other measures include more training for health staff members on the vertical birth method common among indigenous women and teaching the Quiche language to health professionals, Amnesty International said. But the human rights group said Peruvian women and health professionals have complained that the measures are not being implemented effectively. For example, the rights group said, even though the number of waiting houses has increased more than threefold in the past eight years, only half of them are in rural areas. The agency also contends that training for health professionals on the vertical birth method is not sufficiently widespread. According to Peru's Human Rights ombudsperson, more than 45 percent of health staff last year said they had not received appropriate training, Amnesty International said. "Official initiatives to reduce maternal mortality are good news," Garcia said. "However, lack of clear responsibilities for implementing them and the absence of effective resourcing and monitoring puts any initiative in great jeopardy." Though Peru's rate of maternal deaths is high, it pales in comparison to sub-Saharan Africa, which has about 900 deaths for each 100,000 births, the United Nations says. For Africa as a whole, the number is 820. The highest rates were in Sierra Leone, with 2,000, and Afghanistan, with 1,900. Latin America and the Caribbean average 130 deaths per 100,000 births, the United Nations says, with the lowest rates in Chile, Costa Rica and Cuba. Worldwide, there were an average of 400 deaths for each 100,000 births in the year 2000, the United Nations says. The lowest rates were in Iceland, with zero, and Austria, with four per 100,000 births. The United States had 11 deaths per 100,000 births in 2005, the United Nations says. CNN's Stephanie Busari contributed to this report.

The report, *“Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru,”* found that hundreds of poor, rural and Indigenous pregnant women are dying because they are denied the same health services available to other women in the country. It also concluded that the government’s response to the problem has been inadequate.

In wealthy, developed nations, only nine women die for every 100,000 births.

According to figures from Peru’s Ministry of Health, the five leading causes of pregnancy-related deaths in the country are hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, infection, complications following abortion and obstructed birth.

“The rates of maternal mortality in Peru are scandalous,” Amnesty International’s Peru researcher, Nuria Garcia, said in a written statement. “The fact that so many women are dying from preventable causes is a human rights violation.

“The Peruvian state is simply ignoring its obligation to provide adequate maternal health care to all women, regardless of who they are and where they live.”

Garcia added: “Health services for pregnant women in Peru are like a lottery: If you are poor and Indigenous, the chances are you will always lose.”

The report said pregnant women in Peru die because they lack access to emergency obstetric care, maternal health information and health staff members who speak Indigenous languages such as Quechua—a native Andean language spoken by some 5 million people in Peru.

According to the report, 27 percent of pregnancy-related deaths occurred during pregnancy, 26 percent during childbirth itself and 46 percent during the first six weeks after giving birth.

A 2007 Census of Indigenous People showed that 60 percent lacked access to a health facility, Amnesty International said.

The report noted that the Peruvian government has introduced policies aimed at reducing maternal mortality rates, including increasing the number of maternal waiting houses—rooms where pregnant women who live far from health centers can stay.

Other measures include providing more training for health staff members in the vertical birth method common among Indigenous women and teaching the Quiche language to health professionals, Amnesty International said.

However, the human rights group said Peruvian women and health professionals have complained that the measures are not being implemented effectively.

For example, although the number of waiting houses has more than tripled over the past eight years, only half are located in rural areas, the group said. It also contends that training for health professionals in the vertical birth method is not sufficiently widespread.

According to Peru’s human rights ombudsperson, more than 45 percent of health staff members said last year that they had not received appropriate training, Amnesty International reported.

“Official initiatives to reduce maternal mortality are good news,” Garcia said. “However, lack of clear responsibilities for implementing them and the absence of effective resourcing and monitoring puts any initiative in great jeopardy.”

Although Peru’s maternal mortality rate is high, it pales in comparison with that of sub-Saharan Africa, which records about 900 deaths for every 100,000 births, according to the United Nations. For Africa as a whole, the figure is 820. The highest rates were reported in Sierra Leone, with 2,000 deaths per 100,000 births, and Afghanistan, with 1,900.

Worldwide, there was an average of 400 deaths for every 100,000 births in 2000, according to the United Nations. The lowest rates were in Iceland, with zero, and Austria, with four deaths per 100,000 births.

The United States recorded 11 deaths per 100,000 births in 2005, the United Nations says.

**LONDON, England (CNN) —** The author of an Amnesty International investigation into maternal mortality in Peru has described the country’s death rate among pregnant women as outrageous.

The report, titled *“Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru,”* concluded that hundreds of pregnant women—particularly those who are poor, Indigenous or living in rural communities—die because they do not receive the same healthcare available to other Peruvian women. It also found that the government has failed to respond adequately.

Official Peruvian statistics estimate that 185 women die in childbirth for every 100,000 births. The United Nations places the figure considerably higher, at 240 per 100,000, making Peru’s maternal mortality rate one of the worst in the Americas. By comparison, wealthy developed countries record only nine maternal deaths per 100,000 births.

Data from Peru’s Ministry of Health identifies five leading causes of pregnancy-related mortality: hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, infection, complications after abortion and obstructed labor.

In a written statement, Amnesty International’s Peru researcher, Nuria Garcia, called the country’s maternal death rate “scandalous.” She said the loss of so many women to preventable conditions amounts to a violation of human rights.

Garcia accused the Peruvian government of disregarding its duty to ensure that every woman receives proper maternal healthcare, irrespective of her identity or place of residence. She compared maternal services in Peru to a game of chance, saying poor and Indigenous women are the ones most likely to lose.

According to the report, women die because they cannot obtain emergency obstetric treatment, lack access to maternal-health information and are unable to communicate with medical workers who do not speak Indigenous languages. One example is Quechua, an Indigenous Andean language spoken by approximately 5 million people in Peru.

The report found that 27 percent of pregnancy-related deaths occurred before labor, 26 percent happened during delivery and 46 percent took place within six weeks after childbirth.

Amnesty International also cited a 2007 Census of Indigenous People showing that 60 percent of Indigenous respondents had no access to a healthcare facility.

The organization acknowledged that Peru’s government has introduced programs intended to lower maternal mortality. These include expanding the number of maternal waiting houses—accommodations where pregnant women from remote locations can stay near medical centers.

Other government efforts have involved providing additional instruction to healthcare workers in vertical childbirth, a delivery practice common among Indigenous women, and teaching health professionals the Quiche language, Amnesty International said.

However, both Peruvian women and medical personnel have reported that these policies are not being carried out successfully, according to the human rights organization.

For instance, Amnesty said the number of maternal waiting houses has grown by more than three times over the past eight years, yet only half are located in rural communities. It also argued that instruction in vertical delivery techniques has not reached enough healthcare workers.

Amnesty cited Peru’s Human Rights ombudsperson as reporting that, during the previous year, more than 45 percent of healthcare employees said they had not been given suitable training.

Garcia welcomed official programs designed to reduce maternal deaths but warned that they could fail without clearly assigned implementation duties, sufficient funding and resources, and effective oversight.

Although Peru’s maternal mortality rate is severe, it remains far below that of sub-Saharan Africa, where the United Nations estimates about 900 deaths for every 100,000 births. Across Africa as a whole, the figure is 820 per 100,000.

The highest national rates were recorded in Sierra Leone, at 2,000 deaths per 100,000 births, and Afghanistan, at 1,900.

For Latin America and the Caribbean, the United Nations gives an average of 130 maternal deaths per 100,000 births. Chile, Costa Rica and Cuba have the region’s lowest rates.

Globally, the average in 2000 was 400 deaths for each 100,000 births, according to the United Nations. Iceland had the lowest rate, with no recorded deaths, followed by Austria with four per 100,000.

In 2005, the United States recorded 11 maternal deaths per 100,000 births, U.N. figures show.

CNN’s Stephanie Busari contributed to the report.

Amnesty International reports that hundreds of poor, rural, and Indigenous women in Peru die during pregnancy or childbirth because they do not have equal access to essential maternal health services. The country’s maternal mortality rate is estimated at between 185 and 240 deaths per 100,000 births—a stark contrast to the rate of approximately nine deaths per 100,000 births in wealthy developed countries.

The leading causes of pregnancy-related deaths in Peru include severe hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, infection, complications from abortion, and obstructed labor. Many of these conditions can be treated or managed successfully when women receive timely, appropriate medical care. Amnesty International therefore argues that these deaths are largely preventable and should be regarded as a violation of human rights. The organization has also criticized the Peruvian government’s response as inadequate, particularly in addressing the deep inequalities that affect marginalized communities.

Several barriers contribute to the crisis. Emergency obstetric care is often unavailable or difficult to reach in remote areas, while many pregnant women lack clear and accessible information about maternal health and available services. Language differences create an additional obstacle: there are too few healthcare workers who speak Indigenous languages such as Quechua. Together, poverty, geographic isolation, limited health infrastructure, and linguistic discrimination leave many Indigenous and rural women without the care they need, placing their health and lives at avoidable risk.

Amnesty International’s report *Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru* examines why pregnancy and childbirth remain life-threatening for many women in Peru, despite improvements in the country’s health system. The report focuses particularly on poor, rural, and Indigenous women, who experience disproportionately high rates of maternal death. It argues that most of these deaths are not inevitable: they result from complications that can often be prevented or treated when women receive timely prenatal care, skilled assistance during childbirth, emergency obstetric treatment, and reliable follow-up services.

Women living in remote communities frequently have to travel long distances to reach a health facility, often without affordable or dependable transportation. Even when they arrive, clinics may lack trained personnel, medicines, blood supplies, equipment, or the capacity to handle emergencies. Administrative requirements and indirect expenses—such as transportation, food, accommodation, and medication—create additional obstacles for families with limited incomes. These barriers can lead to dangerous delays in deciding to seek care, reaching a facility, and receiving appropriate treatment.

The report also emphasizes the effects of discrimination and cultural exclusion. Many Indigenous women do not receive health information in a language they understand, and interpreters are often unavailable. Some encounter disrespectful treatment or medical practices that fail to take account of their customs and preferences. Fear of humiliation, mistreatment, or being unable to communicate with health workers may discourage women from attending prenatal appointments or giving birth in medical facilities.

Amnesty International presents maternal mortality not simply as a public-health problem but as an issue of human rights and social inequality. The unequal availability and quality of maternal healthcare undermine women’s rights to life, health, equality, information, and freedom from discrimination. The burden falls most heavily on groups that have historically been marginalized, revealing serious disparities between urban and rural areas and between wealthier, Spanish-speaking populations and poorer Indigenous communities.

Although the Peruvian government has introduced programs intended to increase access to maternal healthcare, the report concludes that these measures have been insufficiently implemented and monitored. It calls for accessible, adequately funded health services; trained staff and emergency obstetric care in underserved regions; clear health information; effective Indigenous-language interpretation; culturally appropriate treatment; and reliable systems for investigating maternal deaths and holding authorities accountable.

Ultimately, *Fatal Flaws* argues that hundreds of women die because Peru has failed to remove foreseeable and preventable barriers to care. By allowing poverty, geography, ethnicity, and language to determine whether pregnant women receive life-saving treatment, the state fails to meet its human rights obligations. Reducing maternal mortality therefore requires not only medical reforms but also sustained action against discrimination, exclusion, and inequality.

counterfactuals.output:
# Amnesty report highlights deadly barriers to maternal care in Peru

**Lima, Peru** — Poor, rural and Indigenous women in Peru face preventable obstacles to lifesaving pregnancy care, contributing to one of Latin America’s highest maternal mortality rates, Amnesty International said in a report.

The report, **“Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru,”** said government figures available at the time placed the country’s maternal mortality ratio at about **185 deaths for every 100,000 live births**. That amounted to roughly **two to three women dying each day** from complications related to pregnancy and childbirth.

Most of those deaths were preventable, Amnesty said.

The leading direct causes included **severe bleeding, pregnancy-related high blood pressure such as pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, infections and complications from unsafe abortions**. Delays in recognizing emergencies, reaching a medical facility and receiving appropriate treatment increased the risk.

### Rural and Indigenous women face greatest danger

The national figure masked deep inequalities, according to the report. Women in poor Andean and Amazonian communities were much less likely than women in Lima and other cities to receive prenatal care, give birth with trained medical personnel or gain timely access to emergency obstetric services.

Amnesty documented a series of barriers, including long distances to health centers, shortages of staff and equipment, transportation costs, informal fees and demands for identification documents. Some women also reported being treated disrespectfully or being unable to communicate with health workers because services were not available in Indigenous languages such as Quechua.

Cultural differences could also discourage women from seeking care. In some facilities, women were expected to give birth lying down rather than in the upright position traditionally preferred in many Indigenous communities. Family members were not always allowed to accompany them.

“Whether a woman lives or dies in pregnancy and childbirth should not depend on where she lives, how much money she has or what language she speaks,” Amnesty said in presenting its findings.

The organization argued that maternal mortality was not only a public health crisis but also a **human rights issue**, reflecting discrimination and unequal access to care.

### Government points to progress

Peruvian authorities said they had taken steps to reduce maternal deaths, including expanding subsidized health insurance for low-income families, increasing prenatal care, creating maternity waiting homes near hospitals and promoting culturally adapted services such as vertical childbirth.

The government had also made maternal health a national priority and committed itself to the United Nations Millennium Development Goal of reducing maternal mortality by three-quarters by 2015.

Officials pointed to evidence that maternal deaths had declined over time. Amnesty acknowledged those efforts but said progress was uneven and that policies were often undermined by inadequate funding, poor implementation and weak accountability at the regional and local levels.

The group called on Peru to guarantee free and accessible maternal health services, improve emergency transportation and referral systems, train health workers to provide respectful and culturally appropriate care, and investigate preventable deaths.

Without those changes, Amnesty warned, the women most at risk would continue to be those with the least political and economic power.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on why poor, rural, and Indigenous pregnant women in Peru face exceptionally high rates of preventable maternal death, using findings and quotations from Amnesty International researcher Nuria Garcia.
counterfactuals.output:
## Why maternal death falls disproportionately on poor, rural and Indigenous women in Peru

Amnesty International’s investigation **_Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru_** found that most maternal deaths in Peru were preventable, but that poverty, geography, ethnicity and gender combined to keep many women from receiving timely obstetric care. The report was published in 2009, so its figures describe conditions documented during that period rather than Peru’s current maternal-mortality rate.

Amnesty researcher **Nuria García** summarized the central finding starkly: **“Women are dying because they face discrimination and are denied access to adequate health care.”** She also described Peru’s maternal-mortality problem as a human-rights issue, not merely a medical one: **“The fact that women are dying needlessly, and that the poor and marginalized are disproportionately affected, is a human rights violation that the Peruvian government must address.”**

### A preventable medical emergency

The direct causes of maternal death—including severe bleeding, hypertensive disorders, infection and complications of unsafe abortion or obstructed labour—are generally treatable when women can obtain skilled attendance, emergency obstetric care, blood transfusions and prompt referral. Amnesty therefore argued that the exceptional death rate among disadvantaged women resulted largely from failures in access and treatment rather than from unavoidable complications.

At the time of the investigation, Peru’s national average concealed dramatic regional inequalities. Predominantly rural and Indigenous departments such as **Huancavelica** recorded maternal-mortality levels several times those seen in Lima. Women in rural areas were also much less likely to give birth in a health facility or with a skilled attendant.

### Distance and lack of emergency transport

Many rural communities were hours from the nearest adequately equipped facility. Roads were poor, transport was unavailable or unaffordable, and ambulances were scarce. A woman developing a haemorrhage or eclampsia could therefore die while her family searched for transport, travelled to a clinic or waited to be transferred to a hospital.

Local health posts frequently lacked personnel, medicines, blood supplies and the capacity to perform emergency surgery. The referral system could require women to move between several facilities before receiving definitive care—delays that are often fatal in obstetric emergencies.

### Poverty and hidden charges

Although Peru had introduced public-insurance and free-maternity programmes, Amnesty found that women were still sometimes asked to pay for medicines, tests, supplies, transport or documents. For a household surviving on subsistence farming or informal work, even a relatively small charge could postpone care.

Administrative obstacles also excluded some of the poorest women. Enrolment might require identity papers, proof of poverty or repeated travel to government offices. García’s findings emphasized the gap between formal entitlement and practical access: services described as free were not necessarily free at the point when a woman urgently needed them.

### Discrimination against Indigenous women

Language and racial discrimination were major barriers. Many women spoke Quechua or another Indigenous language, while health information, consent procedures and clinical instructions were provided primarily in Spanish. Interpreters were often unavailable.

Women interviewed by Amnesty reported humiliation, scolding or dismissive treatment by health workers. Some believed they would be treated badly because they were Indigenous, rural, poorly dressed or unable to speak Spanish. Such experiences discouraged prenatal visits and made women reluctant to return to a facility for delivery.

This distrust had material consequences: warning signs might not be identified during pregnancy, and women could delay seeking help until a complication became critical.

### Services that ignored Indigenous culture

Amnesty also found that institutional care was often organized without regard for Indigenous birthing practices. Women could be required to give birth lying horizontally rather than in the upright position customary in many Andean communities; relatives or traditional birth attendants might be excluded; and preferences concerning food, clothing, privacy or treatment of the placenta could be dismissed.

These practices made facilities feel coercive rather than protective. Peru had begun introducing culturally adapted services, including vertical-birth options, but implementation was uneven. Amnesty stressed that cultural accommodation must accompany—not replace—safe clinical care.

### Weak accountability and poor information

Maternal deaths were not always investigated adequately, and families had limited means to challenge negligence or discrimination. Amnesty also found that women were often poorly informed about free services, danger signs in pregnancy and where to seek emergency help. Information campaigns did not consistently reach isolated communities or appear in Indigenous languages.

The result was a cycle in which preventable deaths among politically marginalized women attracted insufficient scrutiny, allowing the same failures to recur.

## Conclusion

Amnesty’s conclusion was that Peru’s maternal deaths were distributed according to social power. A prosperous, Spanish-speaking urban woman was far more likely to reach a functioning hospital and be treated respectfully than a poor Quechua-speaking woman living in a remote Andean community. Geography mattered, but geography was intensified by poverty, underfunded facilities, language exclusion, racism, hidden costs and weak accountability.

García therefore framed the solution as a government obligation: Peru needed not only more clinics, but also reliable emergency referral and transport, genuinely free care, Indigenous-language information, culturally appropriate services, respectful treatment and investigation of every preventable death. Without those measures, a formally universal health system would continue to leave the women at greatest risk least able to use it.

**Primary source:** Amnesty International, *Fatal Flaws: Barriers to Maternal Health in Peru* (2009), with accompanying statements by Peru researcher Nuria García.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed international news story comparing Peru’s maternal mortality rate with rates in developed countries, Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, and the rest of the world.
counterfactuals.output:
**Peru’s maternal mortality remains far above wealthy nations, but below regional and global averages**

*By International News Desk*

**LIMA, Peru —** A woman giving birth in Peru faces a substantially higher risk of dying from pregnancy-related causes than a woman in most wealthy countries, although Peru’s maternal mortality rate remains lower than the averages for Latin America, the world and especially sub-Saharan Africa.

The latest internationally comparable estimates published by United Nations agencies put Peru’s maternal mortality ratio at about **69 deaths for every 100,000 live births in 2020**. The maternal mortality ratio measures deaths during pregnancy, childbirth or within 42 days after a pregnancy ends, when the cause is related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management.

That compares with approximately:

- **13 deaths per 100,000 live births in high-income countries**
- **88 in Latin America and the Caribbean**
- **223 worldwide**
- **545 in sub-Saharan Africa**

The figures come from estimates produced by the World Health Organization, UNICEF, the United Nations Population Fund, the World Bank Group and the U.N. Department of Economic and Social Affairs. Because death registration and reporting systems differ, the agencies use statistical modeling to make countries more comparable. The estimates also carry uncertainty ranges and should not be treated as exact counts.

### A wide gap with developed countries

Peru’s ratio means its estimated maternal death rate was more than **five times the high-income-country average**. The difference reflects large disparities in access to timely obstetric care, emergency surgery, blood transfusions, intensive care, skilled birth attendants and prenatal monitoring.

In many developed health systems, maternal mortality ratios remain in the single digits or low teens. Australia and New Zealand, for example, had a regional estimate of only a few deaths per 100,000 births, while Europe and North America as a group were around the low teens.

Even wealthy countries, however, do not perform equally. The United States has reported a much higher maternal mortality rate than many European countries, and racial and socioeconomic disparities persist across rich nations. Differences in definitions and data-collection methods also complicate direct comparisons between national statistics.

Peru’s challenge is not simply national availability of health services, public-health specialists say, but whether those services can be reached quickly and safely. Women in remote Andean and Amazonian communities may need to travel hours to reach a facility capable of handling hemorrhage, severe hypertension, sepsis or an obstructed labor.

Language barriers, poverty, shortages of specialists, weak referral networks and distrust of health institutions can further delay treatment.

### Better than the Latin American average, but progress is fragile

Peru’s estimated ratio of 69 was lower than the **Latin American and Caribbean average of 88**, placing it ahead of several countries in a region where progress has slowed or reversed.

Latin America has relatively high rates of hospital delivery and prenatal care compared with poorer regions of the world. Yet preventable maternal deaths continue because of uneven quality of care, overcrowded facilities, delayed referrals and deep inequality between urban and rural populations.

The COVID-19 pandemic intensified those weaknesses. Lockdowns, transportation disruptions, staff shortages and fear of infection kept some pregnant women away from clinics. Health systems redirected workers and hospital capacity toward pandemic care, while Peru experienced one of the world’s heaviest COVID-19 death burdens relative to its population.

Nationally reported maternal-death counts may show sharper year-to-year changes than the U.N.’s modeled ratio. The two kinds of data serve different purposes: national surveillance can identify recent emergencies, while U.N. estimates are designed for cross-country comparison.

### Sub-Saharan Africa carries the greatest burden

The contrast with sub-Saharan Africa is stark. The region’s 2020 maternal mortality ratio was estimated at **545 deaths per 100,000 live births**, nearly eight times Peru’s rate and more than 40 times the high-income average.

Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for roughly **seven in every 10 maternal deaths worldwide**, despite representing a much smaller share of global births. In the countries with the weakest health systems, women may face shortages of midwives, doctors, medicines, blood supplies and operating rooms. Conflict, displacement, food insecurity and high rates of adolescent pregnancy add to the danger.

A ratio of 545 does not mean that all African countries have the same level of risk. The continent includes countries that have made major improvements as well as fragile and conflict-affected states where the ratio exceeds 1,000 deaths per 100,000 births.

Peru, by comparison, has a broader health-care network, higher average incomes and greater institutional capacity. But its national figure can conceal local conditions that resemble those of much poorer countries, particularly in isolated districts where emergency treatment is difficult to obtain.

### Peru and the rest of the world

Globally, the maternal mortality ratio stood at about **223 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2020**, more than three times Peru’s level. That world average is heavily influenced by high mortality in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia.

Peru’s rate was therefore comparatively favorable when set against the world as a whole, but it remained far above the level expected in countries with universal, consistently accessible maternity care.

The comparison can be summarized this way:

| Area | Estimated maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, 2020 |
|---|---:|
| High-income countries | About 13 |
| Peru | About 69 |
| Latin America and the Caribbean | About 88 |
| World | About 223 |
| Sub-Saharan Africa | About 545 |

The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals call for the global ratio to fall below **70 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030**, with no country exceeding 140. Peru’s 2020 estimate was just inside the global target, but health experts caution that meeting a numerical threshold nationally does not guarantee safe care for every community.

### Most maternal deaths are preventable

The leading direct causes of maternal death worldwide include severe bleeding, hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia, infections, complications from delivery and unsafe abortion. Indirect causes—including heart disease, anemia, diabetes and infectious diseases—can also become more dangerous during pregnancy.

Many deaths can be prevented through relatively well-established interventions: regular prenatal care, skilled attendance at birth, rapid access to cesarean delivery when necessary, safe blood transfusions, antibiotics, magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia, postpartum monitoring and access to contraception.

For Peru, reducing the gap with developed countries will require more than increasing the number of women who enter the health system. It will also require improving the quality and cultural acceptability of care, strengthening emergency transportation and referrals, and ensuring that rural and Indigenous women receive the same protections as women in major cities.

Peru’s maternal mortality ratio shows that the country performs better than the Latin American and global averages. But the fivefold divide separating it from wealthy countries underscores a central reality of maternal health: whether pregnancy becomes life-threatening still depends heavily on where a woman lives, how quickly she can reach care and whether the health system is prepared to respond.

*Sources: World Health Organization, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank Group and U.N. Population Division, “Trends in Maternal Mortality 2000 to 2020.” Figures are modeled estimates and may differ from national surveillance data.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize Amnesty International’s findings on barriers to maternal healthcare in Peru, including access to emergency obstetric care, Indigenous-language services, maternal waiting houses, and vertical-birth training.
counterfactuals.output:
Amnesty International found that Peru’s reductions in maternal mortality masked severe inequalities affecting poor, rural, and especially Indigenous women. Key barriers included:

- **Emergency obstetric care:** Life-saving services were often too distant, understaffed, poorly equipped, or unavailable around the clock. Weak referral systems, lack of ambulances and transport, difficult terrain, and costs not fully covered by public insurance caused dangerous delays in reaching appropriate care.

- **Indigenous-language services:** Many facilities lacked Quechua- or other Indigenous-language-speaking staff and interpreters. Women could not adequately describe symptoms, understand procedures, give informed consent, or receive health information. Amnesty also documented discriminatory and culturally insensitive treatment, which discouraged women from using institutional services.

- **Maternal waiting houses:** These residences near health facilities could help women from remote communities arrive before labor and avoid emergency travel. However, they were too few, inconsistently funded, and sometimes lacked food, adequate facilities, or support for accompanying relatives and children. Staying away from family, work, and community responsibilities also made them impractical for some women.

- **Vertical-birth training:** Although Peru had adopted guidance allowing culturally preferred upright or vertical birthing positions, implementation was uneven. Many health workers had not been trained, lacked equipment, or continued to insist on horizontal delivery. Thus, the policy often existed on paper without giving women a genuine choice.

Overall, Amnesty concluded that these were not merely logistical shortcomings: they reflected failures to make maternal healthcare **available, accessible, culturally acceptable, and of adequate quality**, with Indigenous and rural women bearing the greatest burden.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a CNN article beginning “LONDON, England (CNN) --” about allegations that Peru’s inadequate maternal health services constitute a human rights violation, citing government, UN, census, and ombudsperson data.
counterfactuals.output:
LONDON, England (CNN) -- Peru is failing to provide many poor and Indigenous women with adequate maternal health care, creating conditions that may amount to violations of their rights to life, health and freedom from discrimination, human rights advocates allege.

The sharpest inequalities are found in remote Andean and Amazonian communities, where women often face long journeys to clinics, shortages of trained staff and blood, language barriers and demands for payment despite government programs intended to provide free care.

Peru’s government says it has expanded insurance coverage, promoted births in health facilities and reduced maternal deaths. Official surveys estimated that the maternal mortality ratio fell from 185 deaths for every 100,000 live births in 2000 to 103 in the period around 2009.

United Nations estimates have at times been higher because they use different methods to account for deaths missed by national reporting systems. U.N. agencies estimated Peru’s maternal mortality ratio at about 240 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2005, underscoring uncertainty over the true scale of the problem.

Human rights groups say the dispute over national figures should not obscure the uneven distribution of risk.

Peru’s 2007 census counted about 28.2 million people, with roughly one-quarter living in rural areas. It also found that millions of Peruvians had learned an Indigenous language in childhood, including about 3.3 million Quechua speakers and nearly half a million Aymara speakers. Those populations are concentrated in regions where poverty is deeper and hospitals, roads and emergency transport are less accessible.

Reports by Peru’s ombudsperson, the Defensoría del Pueblo, have documented gaps in staffing, medicines, equipment, referral systems and culturally appropriate care. Ombudsperson investigations have also recorded cases in which patients insured under public programs were asked to buy supplies or medicines themselves.

Advocates say such barriers can turn treatable complications — including hemorrhage, infection and high blood pressure — into fatal emergencies.

“Maternal death is rarely an unavoidable tragedy,” said one campaigner involved in monitoring Peru’s health system. “It usually reflects a chain of failures: a woman cannot reach a clinic, the clinic lacks staff or blood, and the referral hospital is hours away.”

International human rights standards require governments to make essential health services available and accessible without discrimination. Campaigners argue that Peru’s obligations extend beyond adopting national policies: authorities must ensure that those policies work in practice, particularly for women facing poverty, geographic isolation or discrimination because of language or ethnicity.

Peruvian officials have pointed to measures including the Seguro Integral de Salud, or Comprehensive Health Insurance program; the construction of maternal waiting homes near hospitals; and efforts to train health workers to accommodate traditional birthing practices, such as vertical delivery.

The government has also said that more women are giving birth with skilled assistance and that deaths associated with pregnancy and childbirth have declined substantially.

But women interviewed by rights organizations have described arriving at understaffed facilities, being unable to communicate with Spanish-speaking personnel and having to find their own transportation during emergencies. Some said they delayed seeking care because they feared humiliating or abusive treatment.

The Defensoría del Pueblo has repeatedly urged health authorities to improve emergency obstetric care, guarantee supplies covered by public insurance and strengthen oversight of regional health services.

Specialists say national averages can conceal large regional disparities. In Lima and other urban centers, women generally have greater access to hospitals, specialists and blood banks. In isolated provinces, a health post may be staffed by only a nurse or technician and may be unable to perform a Caesarean section or manage severe bleeding.

The U.N. has identified skilled attendance at birth, functioning referral networks and rapid access to emergency obstetric care as critical to preventing maternal deaths. It has also warned that Indigenous and rural women across Latin America often experience worse health outcomes than national averages suggest.

Rights advocates are calling on Peru to publish more complete data broken down by region, ethnicity, language and income; remove unofficial fees; improve transport and referral systems; and investigate preventable deaths.

They also want women and their families to have effective ways to file complaints and obtain remedies when failures in the health system cause injury or death.

For campaigners, the issue is not whether Peru has made progress, but whether that progress has reached women at greatest risk.

“A falling national mortality rate is important,” the campaigner said. “But preventable deaths among poor, rural and Indigenous women remain a human rights concern when the barriers are known and the state has the means and duty to address them.”
